SECTIONS.label: MFG 1.2–1.3
SECTIONS.title: Functions and their graphs
ideas: A function assigns exactly one output to each input. Inputs form the domain, outputs the range. Notation $y = f(x)$: $f$ is the rule, $x$ the input, $f(x)$ the output. $f(3)$ is a number, not a product.
Functions come four ways: a table, a graph, a formula, a description in words. Move between them fluently; exams ask you to read one and produce another.
Vertical line test: a graph is a function if no vertical line meets it twice. A table is a function if no input repeats with different outputs.

Reading graphs: $f(a)$ is the height at $x = a$. Solving $f(x) = c$ means finding the $x$-values where the height is $c$ (possibly several). Intercepts: $y$-intercept is $f(0)$; $x$-intercepts solve $f(x) = 0$.
Increasing/decreasing, maximum/minimum values, and where $f(x) > 0$ are all read off the graph as intervals of $x$.
Evaluate expressions like $f(a+h)$ by substituting the entire input for every $x$ and simplifying; keep parentheses.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 1.4–1.5
SECTIONS.title: Slope, rate of change, and linear functions
ideas: Average rate of change of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$: the slope of the line through the two points. Units are output units per input unit.
A linear function has a constant rate of change: $f(x) = b + mx$ (Yoshiwara's order) or $y = mx + b$. $m$ is the slope, $b$ the starting value ($y$-intercept).
Find a line from two points: slope first, then point–slope $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$. From a table: check that equal steps in $x$ give equal steps in $y$; if so it is linear.
Intercepts of a line: $y$-intercept $(0,b)$, $x$-intercept $(-b/m, 0)$. Parallel lines share slope; perpendicular slopes multiply to $-1$.
In context: slope tells "how much $y$ changes per one unit of $x$"; the intercept is the value when $x = 0$. Always write the sentence with units.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 2.1–2.2
SECTIONS.title: Nonlinear models and the basic functions
ideas: Many quantities are not linear. Build a model from a geometric or verbal relationship, then use the graph or algebra: area of a square from its perimeter $A = (P/4)^2$, volume of a box from its side, revenue from price.

Solve nonlinear equations by extraction of roots ($x^2 = 20 \Rightarrow x = \pm\sqrt{20}$), by factoring, or graphically (intersection of $y = f(x)$ with $y = c$). Keep both roots unless the context excludes one.

Library of basic functions you must know by shape, domain and range: $y = x^2$, $x^3$, $\sqrt{x}$, $\sqrt[3]{x}$, $1/x$, $1/x^2$, $|x|$. Know which are even/odd, increasing/decreasing, and their asymptotes.
Piecewise functions use different formulas on different intervals; evaluate with the piece whose condition holds. A jump where the pieces do not meet means the graph is discontinuous there.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 2.3
SECTIONS.title: Transformations of graphs
ideas: Starting from a basic graph $y = f(x)$: $f(x) + k$ shifts up $k$; $f(x - h)$ shifts right $h$ (note the sign); $af(x)$ stretches vertically by $a$ (compresses if $0
Order matters: apply stretches and reflections before shifts. $g(x) = -2(x+3)^2 + 4$: shift left 3, stretch by 2, reflect over the $x$-axis, shift up 4. Vertex $(-3, 4)$.
Read the transformation from a graph by locating where the "anchor" point of the parent (vertex, corner, origin) landed and how the heights scaled.
Transformations move the domain and range along: $\sqrt{x-2} - 5$ has domain $[2,\infty)$ and range $[-5,\infty)$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 2.5–2.6
SECTIONS.title: Absolute value, domain, and range
ideas: $|x|$ is the distance from $x$ to 0, so $|x - c|$ is the distance from $x$ to $c$. Graph: a V with corner at $c$. Equations: $|u| = k$ (with $k>0$) means $u = k$ or $u = -k$. Inequalities: $|u| < k \iff -k < u < k$; $|u| > k \iff u < -k \text{ or } u > k$.
Domain from a formula: exclude values that make a denominator zero or an even root negative; everything else is allowed. Write the answer in interval notation.
Range is easiest from the graph: the set of heights reached. Use transformations of the basic functions, or the vertex of a parabola.
In applications the domain is also limited by sense: lengths are positive, people are whole numbers, time starts at 0.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 3.1
SECTIONS.title: Variation
ideas: Direct variation: $y = kx^n$: $y$ scales with a power of $x$; the graph passes through the origin. Doubling $x$ multiplies $y$ by $2^n$.
Inverse variation: $y = k/x^n$: as $x$ grows, $y$ shrinks; the graph never touches the axes.
Find $k$ from one data point, then use the formula. Check a table for variation by testing whether $y/x^n$ (direct) or $yx^n$ (inverse) is constant.
Scaling arguments: if $y \propto x^2$ and $x$ triples, $y$ becomes $9$ times as large; if $y \propto 1/x^2$, it becomes $1/9$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 3.2–3.4
SECTIONS.title: Exponents, roots, radicals, and rational exponents
ideas: Laws: $a^ma^n = a^{m+n}$, $a^m/a^n = a^{m-n}$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$, $(ab)^n = a^nb^n$, $a^0 = 1$, $a^{-n} = 1/a^n$. Negative exponents mean reciprocals, not negative numbers.
Radicals are exponents: $\sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n}$ and $a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m$. Evaluate $8^{2/3}$ as $(\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 4$.
Even roots of negatives are not real; odd roots are fine. $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$.
Solve power equations by isolating the power and applying the reciprocal exponent: $x^{3/2} = 27 \Rightarrow x = 27^{2/3} = 9$. Check for extraneous solutions with even powers.
Simplify radicals by pulling out perfect powers; rationalize denominators when asked.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 4.1–4.2
SECTIONS.title: Exponential growth, decay, and exponential functions
ideas: Exponential change multiplies by the same factor each period: $A(t) = A_0 b^t$ with growth factor $b = 1 + r$ (growth) or $b = 1 - r$ (decay). Percent change per period, not a fixed amount.
Linear vs exponential from a table: constant differences mean linear; constant ratios mean exponential.
$f(x) = ab^x$ with $b>0$, $b\ne1$: domain all reals, range $(0,\infty)$, horizontal asymptote $y = 0$, $y$-intercept $a$. $b>1$ increases; $0<b<1$ decreases. Larger $b$ is steeper.
Find $a$ and $b$ from two points: divide the equations to eliminate $a$, solve for $b$, then back-substitute.
Solve $b^x = b^y$ by matching bases: $8^x = 32 \Rightarrow 2^{3x} = 2^5 \Rightarrow x = 5/3$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 4.3–4.4
SECTIONS.title: Logarithms and their properties
ideas: A logarithm is an exponent: $\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$. $\log_2 8 = 3$ because $2^3 = 8$. $\log x$ means base 10; $\ln x$ means base $e$.
Use logs to solve for an exponent: $3^x = 20 \Rightarrow x = \log_3 20 = \dfrac{\log 20}{\log 3} \approx 2.727$ (change of base).

Properties (products become sums, quotients differences, powers multipliers): $\log_b(MN) = \log_bM + \log_bN$; $\log_b(M/N) = \log_bM - \log_bN$; $\log_b M^p = p\log_bM$. Also $\log_b b = 1$, $\log_b 1 = 0$, $b^{\log_b x} = x$.
There is no rule for $\log(M + N)$. $\log(x+2) \ne \log x + \log 2$.
Logs of numbers $\le 0$ are undefined; the argument must be positive.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 4.5
SECTIONS.title: Exponential models
ideas: Doubling time and half-life characterize exponential growth and decay: $A(t) = A_0\,2^{t/D}$ or $A(t) = A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/H}$.
Convert between forms: $2^{t/D} = b^t$ with $b = 2^{1/D}$; conversely $D = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log b}$.
Fit an exponential to two data points (divide to find $b$), then answer questions with logs: "when does it reach 10,000?" means solve $A_0b^t = 10000$.
Compound interest: $A = P(1 + r/n)^{nt}$; continuous compounding $A = Pe^{rt}$ (§5.3).

SECTIONS.label: MFG 5.1
SECTIONS.title: Inverse functions
ideas: The inverse $f^{-1}$ undoes $f$: if $f(a) = b$ then $f^{-1}(b) = a$. Inputs and outputs swap, so the domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$. The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of $f$ across $y = x$.
Find a formula: write $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, solve for $y$. Check with $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$.
Only one-to-one functions (horizontal line test) have inverses. $x^2$ fails; restrict to $x \ge 0$ and the inverse is $\sqrt x$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 5.2–5.3
SECTIONS.title: Logarithmic functions and the natural base
ideas: $y = \log_b x$ is the inverse of $y = b^x$: domain $(0,\infty)$, range all reals, vertical asymptote $x = 0$, passes through $(1,0)$ and $(b,1)$. Increasing for $b>1$, slowly.
$e \approx 2.718$ is the natural base; $\ln x = \log_e x$. $e^x$ and $\ln x$ are inverses: $e^{\ln x} = x$, $\ln e^x = x$.
Continuous growth $A = A_0e^{kt}$ with continuous rate $k$; the ordinary growth factor is $b = e^k$, so $k = \ln b$. Doubling time $= \ln 2/k$.
Solve exponential equations with $\ln$: $e^{0.3t} = 5 \Rightarrow t = \ln 5/0.3$. Solve log equations by rewriting in exponential form; reject solutions that make any log argument $\le 0$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 6.1–6.3
SECTIONS.title: Quadratic functions: factors, roots, and parabolas
ideas: $x$-intercepts of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ are the solutions of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$. Factor when possible ($x^2 - 5x + 6 = (x-2)(x-3)$); otherwise complete the square or use the quadratic formula. The discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$ tells how many real roots: positive two, zero one, negative none.
Vertex at $x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}$ (midway between the roots); the vertex is the maximum if $a<0$, minimum if $a>0$. Vertex form $y = a(x-h)^2 + k$ shows the vertex $(h,k)$ directly.
Graph a parabola from its intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry $x = h$. Range: $[k,\infty)$ or $(-\infty,k]$.
Factored form $y = a(x - r_1)(x - r_2)$ is fastest when the roots are known. Applications: maximum revenue or area, projectile height.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 7.1–7.2
SECTIONS.title: Polynomial functions and their graphs
ideas: A polynomial $a_nx^n + \dots + a_0$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $a_n$. End behavior depends only on the leading term: even degree, both ends go the same way (up if $a_n>0$); odd degree, opposite ways (like $x^3$ if $a_n>0$).

Zeros come from factors: $(x - r)^k$ gives a zero at $r$ of multiplicity $k$. Odd multiplicity crosses the axis; even multiplicity touches and turns. A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ real zeros and at most $n-1$ turning points.

To sketch: find zeros and multiplicities, the $y$-intercept, end behavior; then connect smoothly. To write a formula from a graph: use the zeros for factors and one extra point to find the constant $a$.
Products and powers of binomials: expand carefully; $(x-2)^3 \ne x^3 - 8$.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 7.3
SECTIONS.title: Complex numbers
ideas: $i = \sqrt{-1}$, $i^2 = -1$. Every complex number is $a + bi$. Square roots of negatives: $\sqrt{-20} = 2i\sqrt5$.
Add and subtract componentwise; multiply like binomials and replace $i^2$ with $-1$; divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate $a - bi$ (which makes the denominator $a^2 + b^2$).

Quadratics with negative discriminant have two complex conjugate roots: $x^2 - 2x + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1 \pm 2i$. Every polynomial of degree $n$ has exactly $n$ zeros counting multiplicity and complex zeros.

SECTIONS.label: MFG 7.4–7.5
SECTIONS.title: Rational functions and equations with algebraic fractions
ideas: $f(x) = \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}$. Vertical asymptotes where $q = 0$ and $p \ne 0$ (after cancelling common factors; a cancelled factor makes a hole instead). $x$-intercepts where $p = 0$.
Horizontal asymptote from the degrees: $\deg p < \deg q$: $y = 0$; equal: $y =$ ratio of leading coefficients; $\deg p > \deg q$: none (the graph follows the quotient).
Sketch using intercepts, asymptotes, and a sign check in each interval. Near a vertical asymptote the graph shoots up or down; test a point on each side.
Solve equations with fractions by multiplying through by the LCD, then check that no solution makes a denominator zero (extraneous solutions).

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 1.1–1.3
SECTIONS.title: Angles, triangles, similar triangles, and circles
ideas: Angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$. Right triangles obey the Pythagorean theorem $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$. Isosceles triangles have equal base angles.

Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides: corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Set up proportions with matching positions (short/short = long/long). Common sources: parallel lines, shadows, nested right triangles.
Special right triangles: $45^\circ$–$45^\circ$–$90^\circ$ sides $1 : 1 : \sqrt2$; $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ sides $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$.
Circles: circumference $2\pi r$, area $\pi r^2$; the equation of a circle centered at $(h,k)$ is $(x-h)^2 + (y-k)^2 = r^2$. Distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in coordinates.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 2.1–2.3
SECTIONS.title: Trigonometric ratios and solving right triangles
ideas: For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$ (SOH-CAH-TOA). The ratios depend only on the angle, not the triangle's size (similarity).

Exact values: $\sin30^\circ = \tfrac12$, $\cos30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2$, $\tan30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$; $\sin45^\circ = \cos45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}2$, $\tan45^\circ = 1$; $\sin60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}2$, $\cos60^\circ = \tfrac12$, $\tan60^\circ = \sqrt3$.

Solve a triangle = find all sides and angles. From one side and one acute angle: the other angle is $90^\circ - \theta$; use the ratio that links the known side to the wanted side. From two sides: find the third by Pythagoras and an angle by an inverse ratio ($\theta = \tan^{-1}(\text{opp}/\text{adj})$).
Applications: angle of elevation/depression, ladders, ramps. Draw, label the right angle, mark which side is opposite the known angle.
Cofunctions: $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta)$.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 3.1–3.3
SECTIONS.title: Obtuse angles, Law of Sines, Law of Cosines
ideas: Coordinate definitions extend the ratios to any angle: for a point $(x,y)$ at distance $r$ from the origin on the terminal side, $\sin\theta = y/r$, $\cos\theta = x/r$, $\tan\theta = y/x$. Obtuse angles have negative cosine and positive sine: $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$, $\cos(180^\circ - \theta) = -\cos\theta$.

Law of Sines $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$: use with two angles and a side (AAS/ASA) or two sides and a non-included angle (SSA, the ambiguous case: check for a second triangle with $180^\circ - B$).
Law of Cosines $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$: use with two sides and the included angle (SAS) or three sides (SSS). It reduces to Pythagoras when $C = 90^\circ$.
Area of any triangle: $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 4.1–4.3
SECTIONS.title: Angles, rotation, and the graphs of trigonometric functions
ideas: Angles in standard position open counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis; negative angles go clockwise; coterminal angles differ by $360^\circ$. The reference angle is the acute angle to the $x$-axis; trig values of any angle equal those of its reference angle up to sign, and the quadrant fixes the sign (All Students Take Calculus: I all positive, II sine, III tangent, IV cosine).
On the unit circle $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ is the point at angle $\theta$. So $\sin$ and $\cos$ are periodic with period $360^\circ$, bounded between $-1$ and $1$.

Graphs: $y = \sin\theta$ starts at 0 rising; $y = \cos\theta$ starts at 1; both have amplitude 1 and period $360^\circ$. $y = \tan\theta$ has period $180^\circ$ with vertical asymptotes at $\pm90^\circ$.
Use the graphs to solve $\sin\theta = k$ over a range: two solutions per period for $|k| < 1$, found from the reference angle.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 5.1, 5.3
SECTIONS.title: Algebra with trig ratios and trigonometric identities
ideas: Treat $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ like variables when simplifying: $\sin\theta\cos\theta + 2\sin\theta = \sin\theta(\cos\theta + 2)$. Careful: $\sin 2\theta \ne 2\sin\theta$ and $\sin^2\theta$ means $(\sin\theta)^2$.

Fundamental identities: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ (and its forms $1 - \cos^2\theta = \sin^2\theta$), $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$, $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$.
Prove an identity by transforming one side into the other (usually the messier side): convert everything to sine and cosine, combine fractions, factor, use the Pythagorean identity.
Solve equations by isolating one trig function, using identities to reduce to a single function, then finding all angles in the interval.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 6.1–6.3
SECTIONS.title: Arclength, radians, and the circular functions
ideas: A radian is the angle that cuts an arc equal to the radius. $180^\circ = \pi$ rad, so multiply degrees by $\pi/180$ to get radians. Arclength $s = r\theta$ and sector area $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta$ need $\theta$ in radians.
Know the unit-circle values in radians: $\pi/6 = 30^\circ$, $\pi/4 = 45^\circ$, $\pi/3 = 60^\circ$, $\pi/2 = 90^\circ$, $\pi = 180^\circ$, $3\pi/2 = 270^\circ$, $2\pi = 360^\circ$.
The circular functions $\sin t$, $\cos t$ take a real number $t$ (an arc length on the unit circle) as input, which is what calculus uses. Graphs have period $2\pi$; $\tan t$ has period $\pi$.
Reference numbers work like reference angles: $t$ in QII has reference $\pi - t$, QIII $t - \pi$, QIV $2\pi - t$.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 7.1–7.3
SECTIONS.title: Transformations, the general sinusoid, and solving equations
ideas: General sinusoid $y = A\sin(B(x - h)) + k$ (or cosine): amplitude $|A|$, period $2\pi/B$ (or $360^\circ/B$), horizontal shift $h$, midline $y = k$. Maximum $k + |A|$, minimum $k - |A|$.
Model periodic data (tides, temperature, Ferris wheels): midline is the average of max and min, amplitude is half the difference, period from the cycle, shift from where the cycle starts.
Graph in one period: mark five key points (start, quarter, half, three-quarter, end) using the period, then apply amplitude and midline.
Solve $A\sin(Bx) + k = c$: isolate the sine, find the reference angle, list all solutions of the inner angle in the needed range, then divide by $B$. More solutions appear when $B > 1$.

SECTIONS.label: TRIG 8.2–8.3
SECTIONS.title: Inverse trigonometric functions and the reciprocal functions
ideas: Sine, cosine and tangent are not one-to-one, so their inverses use restricted domains: $\sin^{-1}x$ returns angles in $[-\pi/2, \pi/2]$, $\cos^{-1}x$ in $[0,\pi]$, $\tan^{-1}x$ in $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. Inputs to $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ must lie in $[-1,1]$.
Consequence: $\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only when $\theta$ is in the restricted range. $\sin^{-1}(\sin 150^\circ) = 30^\circ$.
Solving $\sin\theta = k$ over a full circle needs the inverse value and its partner ($180^\circ - $ value for sine, $360^\circ -$ value for cosine, $+180^\circ$ for tangent).

Reciprocal functions: $\sec\theta = 1/\cos\theta$, $\csc\theta = 1/\sin\theta$, $\cot\theta = 1/\tan\theta$; undefined where the denominator is 0. Identities $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$, $1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta$.
Exact evaluations: $\cos(\sin^{-1}\tfrac35)$: draw the right triangle with opposite 3, hypotenuse 5, adjacent 4, so $\tfrac45$.

SECTIONS.label: Quadratic-in-form
SECTIONS.title: Quadratic-in-form equations, trigonometric and algebraic
ideas: An equation is quadratic in form when a substitution $u = (\text{something})$ turns it into $au^2 + bu + c = 0$: $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ with $u = x^2$; $x^{2/3} - x^{1/3} - 6 = 0$ with $u = x^{1/3}$; $2\sin^2\theta - \sin\theta - 1 = 0$ with $u = \sin\theta$.

Solve for $u$ by factoring or the quadratic formula, then undo the substitution for each $u$ value and keep only valid results ($|\sin\theta| \le 1$, radicands non-negative, domain of the original equation).
Trig versions may need an identity first to get a single function: $2\cos^2\theta + \sin\theta = 2$ becomes $2(1 - \sin^2\theta) + \sin\theta = 2$.
Report trig solutions for the required interval, using reference angles, and check for solutions where you divided by something.
